title: Count Pairs of Equal Substrings With Minimum Difference
statement:
You are given two 0-indexed strings `firstString` and `secondString` made of lowercase English letters. Call a quadruple of indices `(i, j, a, b)` valid when:

- `0 <= i <= j < firstString.length` and `0 <= a <= b < secondString.length`, and
- the piece of `firstString` from index `i` to index `j` (both included) is the same string as the piece of `secondString` from index `a` to index `b` (both included).

Look at the value `j - a` over all valid quadruples and take its smallest value. Return how many valid quadruples have exactly that smallest `j - a`. If there is no valid quadruple at all, return `0`.
constraints: firstString and secondString contain only lowercase English letters
notes:
## Intuition

Listing every pair of equal substrings is far too slow. The key is that only single letters can reach the minimum. Take any valid quadruple `(i, j, a, b)` whose pieces have length 2 or more. Its first letters agree, so `(i, i, a, a)` is also valid, and its `j - a` value is `i - a`, which is strictly smaller. So every quadruple achieving the minimum is a single matching letter, `firstString[i] === secondString[a]`, with value `i - a`.

For one letter, `i - a` is smallest when `i` is its **first** position in `firstString` and `a` is its **last** position in `secondString`, and that pair is unique. So each letter offers one candidate, and the answer is how many letters tie for the best candidate.

## Approach

1. Fill `first[c]` with the earliest index of letter `c` in `firstString` (scan right to left so the earliest write wins).
2. Fill `last[c]` with the latest index of letter `c` in `secondString` (scan left to right).
3. For each letter present in both strings, compute `diff = first[c] - last[c]`.
4. A smaller `diff` resets `best` and sets `count` to 1; an equal one adds 1 to `count`.
5. Return `count` (still 0 when no letter is shared).

## Example 1, step by step

`firstString = "abcd"`, `secondString = "bccda"`.

| letter | `first` | `last` | `diff` |
|---|---|---|---|
| a | 0 | 4 | -4 |
| b | 1 | 0 | 1 |
| c | 2 | 2 | 0 |
| d | 3 | 3 | 0 |

The smallest `diff` is -4, reached only by `a`, so the answer is `1`: the quadruple `(0, 0, 4, 4)`.

## Complexity

- Time: O(n + m): one pass over each string plus 26 letters.
- Space: O(1): two arrays of 26 entries.

## Pitfalls

- The minimum is over `j - a` (end in the first string, start in the second), not `i - a`; it only coincides with `i - a` for single letters.
- Use the first occurrence in `firstString` but the last occurrence in `secondString`; mixing them up maximises instead.
- `diff` can be negative, so start `best` at `Infinity`, not 0.
- Count ties across different letters; each letter itself contributes at most one quadruple.

## Variables

| Name | Meaning |
|---|---|
| `first` | earliest index of each letter in `firstString`, or -1 |
| `last` | latest index of each letter in `secondString`, or -1 |
| `c` | letter index 0..25 |
| `diff` | the best `j - a` this letter can give |
| `best`, `count` | smallest `diff` so far and how many letters reach it |

narration.4: Scan firstString from right to left, so the last write for each letter is its earliest position.
narration.5: Record this index as the earliest place the letter appears in firstString.
narration.7: Scan secondString from left to right, so the last write for each letter is its latest position.
narration.8: Record this index as the latest place the letter appears in secondString.
narration.10: No candidate seen yet; differences can be negative, so start at Infinity.
narration.12: Each letter offers exactly one best single-letter quadruple.
narration.13: A letter missing from either string cannot form a match.
narration.16: Earliest i minus latest a is the smallest j - a this letter can reach.
narration.17: A new smallest difference replaces the old one...
narration.19: ...and so far only this letter achieves it.
narration.20: Another letter ties the smallest difference.
narration.21: Count it as one more quadruple.
narration.24: The number of letters tied for the minimum is the number of quadruples.
